title: Ibn Fadlan on the Volga
hookLine: an envoy from Baghdad describes the far north, cold and all
tomorrow: why do some groups hold together while others fall apart?

lines: THE FOOD'S WRONG. THE WEATHER'S WRONG.
cards: First week somewhere new: the food's wrong, the weather's wrong, the jokes land differently, and every message home has to choose between brave and honest. How do you describe a place that feels nothing like home?
Ibn Fadlan had to. He went as part of an embassy from the caliph in Baghdad to the king of the Bulghars on the Volga, and he wrote down what he saw, cold and all.

teach.b: His account is blunt. The cold, he writes, was so fierce that his beard froze into a block of ice, and he had to thaw it by a fire.

teach.h: NIGHTS TOO SHORT FOR THE PRAYERS.
teach.b: He records how short the summer nights were there, so short that the evening prayers and the dawn nearly ran into each other.
For a man who prays by the sun, that isn't trivia: the clock of his whole day stopped making sense, and he kept praying anyway, fitting the prayers into a sky that wouldn't keep his hours.
He also describes the peoples he met, their dress, their customs, their funerals, and at times he's openly disgusted. That's in the record too.

teach.h: WHERE HE LOOKS, WHERE HE DOESN'T.
teach.b: Readers learn from where he looks closely and from where disgust takes the place of looking. What makes the account worth reading is the attempt: he wrote what he saw, not what Baghdad expected.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall: “Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance.”

Far north or home, the prayer came with him. So describing a strange place honestly means two things at once: telling the truth about the cold, and remembering that you're the stranger there. The far north.

how: Muslims living or traveling where nights are very short or very long follow scholars' rulings on how to time the prayers; Ibn Fadlan's account is read by historians of the north.

games.q: what does “ibn fadlan on the volga” mean?
o: a merchant's map of the trade roads to China
a poem about a battle on a frozen river
an envoy's honest account of the cold far north

games.q: Ibn Fadlan's north — tap the pairs.

s: Ibn Fadlan's account describes only the peoples he met, not himself
he records his own frozen beard and his prayers in short nights.
he went as part of an embassy from the caliph in Baghdad
to the king of the Bulghars on the Volga.
everything Ibn Fadlan wrote about the peoples he met was fair
at times he's openly disgusted; readers weigh where he looks closely and where he doesn't.

games.q: you move to a new city and want to post about it. what fits Ibn Fadlan at his best?
o: describe what's really there, cold and kind, as the newcomer you are.
post only the good parts, so nobody back home worries.
compare it with home and say which one is better.
games.why: his account is worth reading where he wrote what he saw, and weakest where disgust took the place of looking.

practice: Say out loud, in three plain sentences, what's around you right now: what's cold or warm, what's loud, what's unfamiliar. Use no judging words, only what's there. Then sit with the room you just described.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Fadlan on the Volga: an envoy's blunt account of the far north, frozen beards, short summer nights and peoples new to him.

carryVoice: What stays with you: the far north, told honestly, with you as the stranger. Day 1650, written up.
